Chapter 1. Arriving in a New World Through Food and Curiosity
Picture this: stepping off the plane in a new country. It’s not just about crossing a border, is it? Suddenly, you’re moving to a whole new rhythm. The tiniest things—like the way people say hello or the scent of fresh bread drifting through the air—remind you life here will be different.
If you’d landed in Russia just after the Soviet Union’s collapse, your first days might feel like walking into a living storybook—one filled with old apartment blocks, lively markets, and a pulse that’s both unfamiliar and inviting. You’d feel a bit like an outsider, but also a welcome guest—someone allowed to watch, but not quite part of the scene just yet.
Those first few days? They’re all about small discoveries. The language, with its rolling sounds, feels like trying to solve a puzzle with no picture on the box. Even grocery shopping turns into an adventure. Imagine standing in front of a table stacked high with root vegetables, trying to guess what each one’s called or how to use it. The vendors, bundled up in thick coats, might offer advice—sometimes patient, sometimes just a little amused. You notice the pride in how they handle their food. Here, food isn’t just something to eat—it’s a way to connect the past with the present.
Pretty soon, you realize food’s the fastest way to bridge cultures. A dinner invitation? It’s more than just a meal—it’s a doorway into Russian hospitality. The first time you sit at a Russian table, it can be a little overwhelming, but there’s comfort too. The table’s packed: jars of pickles, slices of dark rye bread, steaming bowls of soup loaded with dill, and platters of cured fish. There’s a rhythm to it all—a dance of toasts and laughter, where every dish has its own story.
One evening, you might find yourself squeezed into a tiny kitchen, watching your host make borscht. The pace is slow, almost soothing. Beets are peeled and grated, onions are chopped, and the soup gently bubbles away. Your host tells you—every family has their own recipe, shaped by memory and place. When the soup’s finally served, the room fills with warmth. And even if you’re still stumbling through the language, you get it—sometimes understanding comes from sharing these everyday rituals, not just from words.
Adapting to life here isn’t really about big dramatic gestures. It’s about saying yes to a cup of tea, tasting a salad you’ve never tried, or joining in a vodka toast. It’s in these little moments that you start to belong. Soon, the city that once felt so daunting begins to feel almost like home. Riding the tram, shopping at the market, cooking in a cramped kitchen—they become part of your new routine. Through food, you find ways to connect, to listen, and to be heard.
In Russia, meals are never just about eating. They’re about gathering, remembering, and making sense of the world with others. The kitchen table becomes the place where stories are swapped and friendships are formed. Slowly, the line between guest and host fades away.
So if you’re open to tasting, listening, and sharing, your journey into Russian life? It truly begins with that very first bite.
